title: Benefit changes, housing promises and bank refund rights
summary:
Spain expands Social Security protection and raises advances for unpaid child support. We examine voting restrictions, housing research and campaign promises, bank refund rights, and new university assessment rules.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Could an unmarried parent qualify for a widow's pension without—

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: —registering as a couple? The new rules allow that, with conditions.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So the shared home matters, not just the paperwork.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For parents with children together, that's a meaningful change.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Good morning! It's Thursday, the twenty-second of October, and this is Spain Daily, from Spanified dot com!

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: I'm Inna, here with Dima. Today: housing promises on the campaign trail, and faster refunds for unauthorised bank payments.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: First, the Social Security changes: who gets more protection, and which payments start later.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: A decree-law expanding Social Security benefits took effect yesterday, El Diario reports. Some provisions begin later. Unregistered unmarried couples with children together can qualify for a widow's pension. They need stable, publicly recognised cohabitation for at least two uninterrupted years immediately before the death.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The decree covers menopause-related leave and protection connected with catastrophes. It also extends support for parents of seriously ill children and victims of gender violence. Some provisions begin over the next couple of months, rather than immediately.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Dima, what's the key condition for an unmarried couple with children?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Two uninterrupted years of living together, right before the death. Registering as a couple isn't required.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Another measure for families: Heraldo reports that advances for unpaid, court-ordered child support rise from November first. The monthly maximum increases from one hundred to three hundred euros per child. These are payments through the public guarantee fund. Current recipients don't need to apply again.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: So a parent already receiving the advance doesn't have to restart the application?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Existing files get reviewed automatically, and the higher maximum applies to each child separately. oh, good

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That removes another application for families already relying on the fund.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: The Supreme Court meets today over voting restrictions affecting about a hundred and sixty thousand naturalised citizens, Europa Press reports. The restrictions concern people naturalised under the grandchildren's law who cannot prove descent from exiles. Submissions are due tomorrow. Yesterday, the Constitutional Court rejected an appeal as premature; the Supreme Court must still rule on the merits.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Hold on. Does today's review leave affected parties just until tomorrow to submit their arguments?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: That's the deadline. The restrictions remain in force while the Supreme Court considers the case.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And the general election is on the twenty-ninth of November. It's still unclear whether they'll be able to vote.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Housing is another election issue, and new research examines who charges more. El Mundo reports that landlords with five or more rental properties charge seven percent higher rents. The EsadecPol study attributes most accumulated rent increases to wider market pressure, rather than large landlords alone.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Huh. So landlord size shows a difference, but doesn't explain most of the rise?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Exactly. You can see a premium from larger portfolios, while the broader market still drives most increases. right

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Which makes a single explanation for rising rents rather hard to defend.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Staying with housing, Partido Popular leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo set out campaign promises yesterday, Europa Press reports. If elected, he promises tax deductions for tenants and owners, and a million homes. His proposed housing package includes a law allowing squatter evictions within forty-eight hours.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's quite a range. Inna, are the promised tax deductions aimed at both sides of a rental contract?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Both tenants and owners. The campaign offer reaches renters, landlords and people hoping to buy.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: The Catalan Socialist Party has offered Comuns, another Catalan party, a revised housing bill, El País reports. The proposal removes purchase limits and focuses on permanent residential use in high-pressure areas. The text isn't agreed. A legal watchdog warned that the earlier version violated property and inheritance rights.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Wait, the focus shifts from how many homes someone buys to how the homes are used?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's the proposed shift, towards homes being used as permanent residences in those high-pressure areas. I see

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: For buyers there, the intended use of a property is central to this version.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And there's a housing agreement in principle in the Basque Country. El País reports a hundred-million-euro deal covering more than five hundred protected homes in San Sebastián. The Basque Government would buy surface rights over the homes from Testa, a Blackstone subsidiary. Signing is expected at the end of this year. That would keep the protection beyond November twenty twenty-eight.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, that's welcome for tenants. The protection would stop those homes moving to market rents?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: That's what the agreement would secure. For the households there, it's protection against that change in rent.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: El País reports a ruling from the EU Court of Justice. Banks must refund unauthorised payments within twenty-four hours, even where the customer was grossly negligent. The bank returns the money first, then claims it back from the customer afterwards.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Even if the customer made the mistake themselves?

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Yes, even then. For example writing the PIN on the card, or dictating a one-time code by phone. Banks can no longer cite that negligence to refuse a refund.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For someone whose account has been emptied, getting the money returned promptly matters while that dispute continues.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Households on the regulated gas tariff face a delayed cost. Heraldo reports that the government's cap limits their rise to about fifteen percent, instead of more than forty-five percent. The difference is deferred for later repayment, with interest. So lower charges now don't erase the underlying cost.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: For business cash payments, an EU ceiling of ten thousand euros begins on July tenth next year, reports Veinte Minutos. Linked transactions count together. Countries can retain lower limits, so Spain's stricter rules can remain. Private transactions between people acting outside a professional activity are exempt.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: So someone paying a business here can't simply assume the European ceiling is their permitted limit?

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Correct. Lower national limits can stay, so the Spanish rules still matter when you're making that payment. mhm

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Off Catalonia, Aemet, Spain's weather agency, is studying possible tropical cyclone formation on October third and fourth, El País reports. A preliminary study suggests record Mediterranean temperatures may have powered the system. Torrential rain occurred without the usual atmospheric trigger. Researchers haven't established whether a cyclone actually formed.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: And university students gain more assessment flexibility. La Vanguardia reports that a decree published today provides at least two exam sittings per subject annually. Resits should allow the full final grade where possible. Universities must also accommodate learning difficulties and students' work and personal circumstances.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Oh, the full grade matters. A second sitting can offer more than just a narrow chance to scrape through.

segments.speaker: Dima
segments.body: Where the subject allows it, yes. That gives the resit a more useful role.

segments.speaker: Inna
segments.body: Today's practical thread: benefits, refunds and bills all turn on who qualifies, and when the change reaches them.
